\section{Unique continuation}
\begin{definition}
  A measurable function $u$ defined in a domain $D$ of the euclidean  $n $-space  is said to have a zero of order $ \alpha >0$        at  $x_0 \in D $   in the $p$-mean ( $1 \leq p\leq \infty  $  ) if
  $$ \int_{|x-x_0|<r}|u|^p dx=O(|r|^{p\alpha+n }). $$
\end{definition}
\begin{remark}
  The usual definition of a zero of order $\alpha  $ corresponds to $p=\infty . $     
\end{remark}
\begin{remark}
  The zero is said to be of infinite order if it is of order $\alpha  $   for all $\alpha >0 $. 
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Heinz]
  Let $r \leq 1 $ and $u $ vanishes outside a compact set contained in $0<|x|<r $, then      
 \begin{equation}
  cr^2 \int_{|x|<r} |x|^{-2 \alpha } |\Delta u|^2 dx \geq \int_{|x|<r} |x|^{- 2 \alpha } \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n |\frac{\partial u}{\partial x^i} |^2+|u|^2 \right] dx.
 \end{equation}
\end{theorem}


Consider first the metric 
$$ a_{ij}dx^idx^j .$$
Fix a point $x_0 \in D $ and denote the distance by $r=|x-x_0| $. Introduce the new tensor (for constant $\nu  $  )
$$ \tilde{a}^{ij}=e^{2 \nu r^2} a^{ij},\quad  \tilde{a}_{ij}=e^{-2 \nu r^2} a_{ij},$$    
and the Laplacian-Beltrami operator
$$ \tilde{A}= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde{a}}} \frac{\partial }{\partial x^i} (\sqrt{\tilde{a}} a^{ij} \frac{\partial }{\partial x^j} )  .$$

Then the new distance $\tilde{r} $ are related to $r $ by (geodesics are the same)
$$ \tilde{r}=\int_{0}^{r} e^{-\nu \sigma ^2} d \sigma . $$    

\begin{theorem}
Denote the sphere by $\tilde{S}_h(x_0) $   with $\tilde{r} <h $ in the metric $d \tilde{s} $. Then 
$$ ch^2 \int_{\tilde{S}_h(x_0)} \tilde{r}^{-2 \alpha } |\tilde{A}u|^2 \sqrt{\tilde{a}} dx \geq \int_{\tilde{S}_h(x_0)} \tilde{r}^{-2 \alpha } \left[ \tilde{a}^{ij}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x^j} +|u|^2   \right] \sqrt{\tilde{a}} dx,$$
where $u $ vanishes outside a compact set of $\tilde{S}_h(x_0) \setminus x_0 $ and $c $ is a constant independent on $u $ and $\alpha  .$              
\end{theorem}

\section{$f$-harmonic maps}

\begin{definition}[$f$-Laplacian, $\ricci_f$]
    $$ \lap_f(u):=\lap u -\la \nabla u,\nabla f \ra  ,$$
    $$ \ricci_f := \ricci +\hess f. $$
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Bochner formula]
 \begin{equation}
   \frac{1}{2} \lap_f |\nabla u|^2=|\hess u|^2+\la \nabla u, \nabla \lap_f u\ra+\ricci_f(\nabla u,\nabla u). 
 \end{equation}
\end{proposition}
Indeed, 
$$ \begin{aligned}
   \frac{1}{2} \lap_f |\nabla u|^2=& \frac{1}{2}\lap |\nabla u|^2-\hess u (\nabla u,\nabla f)\\
   \la \nabla u,\nabla \lap_f u \ra=& \la \nabla u,\nabla \lap u \ra -\hess u(\nabla u,\nabla f)-\hess f(\nabla u,\nabla u).
\end{aligned}  $$
For the first inequality, recall 
$$ \hess u (X,Y)= \la \nabla _X \nabla u,  Y \ra.  $$
The second equality follows from 
$$ \begin{aligned}
    \la \nabla u,\nabla \la \nabla u,\nabla f \ra  \ra=&\nabla u \cdot \la \nabla u,\nabla f \ra  \\
    =& \nabla u \cdot \nabla u \cdot f= \nabla u \cdot \nabla f \cdot u
\end{aligned}  $$
and 
$$ \begin{aligned}
   \hess u(\nabla u,\nabla f)+\hess f(\nabla u,\nabla u)=& \nabla u \cdot \nabla f \cdot u-(\nabla _{\nabla u}\nabla f) u+\nabla u \cdot \nabla   u \cdot f -(\nabla _{\nabla u}\nabla u) f\\
   =&\nabla u \cdot \nabla f \cdot u+\nabla u \cdot \nabla   u \cdot f -(\nabla _{\nabla u}\nabla f) u-(\nabla _{\nabla u}\nabla u) f \\
   =& 2 \la \nabla u,\nabla \la \nabla u,\nabla f \ra  \ra- \nabla u \cdot \la \nabla u,\nabla f \ra.
\end{aligned}  $$


\section{$f$-pseudoharmonic maps}

\begin{equation}
    E_{b,f}(u)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{M}|d_b u|^2 e^{-f} dv_{\theta }
\end{equation}

\np (\textbf{The first variation formula.})

Let $u_t:M \to N$ be a family maps from pseudohermitian manifold $(M, H, \theta ) $ to Riemannian manifold $N$.
Then 
$$ \begin{aligned}
    \frac{d}{dt} E_{b,f}(u_t)=& \int_{M} \la \nabla _{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}} d u_t(e_i),du_t(e_i)  \ra e^{-f} dv_{\theta }\\
    =& \int_{M}^{} \la \nabla _{e_i} \frac{\partial u_t}{\partial t},du_t(e_i)  \ra e^{-f} dv_{\theta }\\
    =& \int_{M}^{} e_i \la V,e^{-f}du(e_i)  \ra -\la V, \nabla _{e_i} (e^{-f}du(e_i))  \ra
    dv_{\theta }\\
    =& \int_{M}  e_i \la V,e^{-f}du(e_i)  \ra dv_{\theta }
    +\int_{M} \la V,  e_i(f) du(e_i) -\nabla _{e_i} du(e_i)\ra e^{-f} 
    dv_{\theta }.
\end{aligned}  $$   
Set 1-form $\eta (X):=\la V,e^{-f}du(X)  \ra$, then  
$$\begin{aligned}
    \delta (\eta )=&-\sum_{A=1}^{2m+1} (\nabla _{e_A} \eta) (e_A)\\
    =& -e_A \la V, e^{-f}du(e_A)  \ra +\la V, e^{-f} du(\nabla _{e_A}e_A)  \ra .
\end{aligned}   $$
It follows that 
$$ \begin{aligned}
    \frac{d}{dt} E_{b,f}(u_t)=& -\int_{M} \delta (\eta )+T\la V , e^{-f}du(T) \ra -\la V , e^{-f} du(\nabla _{T}T) \ra dv_{\theta }\\
    &-\int_{M} \la V, \tau _b (u) \ra e^{-f} dv_{\theta }+\int_{M} \la V, du(\nabla _b f) \ra e^{-f}dv_\theta \\
    =& - \int_{M}\la V, \tau _b (u) -du(\nabla _b f)\ra e^{-f}dv_\theta .
\end{aligned}  $$
Thus $u$ is $f$-pseudoharmonic iff 
\begin{equation}
    \tau _b (u) -du(\nabla _b f)=0,
\end{equation} 
or, locally,
\begin{equation}
    u_{ii }^{\alpha  }-f_i u_{i }^{\alpha }=0, \quad \forall \alpha .
\end{equation}

\np (\textbf{Bochner formula}) 

Note that $|d_b u|^2= \sum_{i,\alpha }^{} (u_{i}^{\alpha })^2$ 
$$ \begin{aligned}
    &\lap_b |d_b u|^2-\la d |d_b u|^2, d_b f \ra\\
   =& \lap_b |d_b u|^2-2u_{ij}^{\alpha }u_{i}^{\alpha }f_j\\
\end{aligned}  $$


\section{Stability of minimal hypersurfaces in a 3-manifold}


\begin{enumerate}
    \item Chen Zhou, \textit{A new proof of Huber's theorem on differential geometry in the large}
    \item Peter Li and Luen-fai Tam,  \textit{Complete Surfaces With Finite Total Curvature}
\end{enumerate}


\begin{theorem}[Huber]
Let $M$ be a connected open Riemann surface and let $\mathrm{d}s^2$ be a complete conformal Riemannian metric( This metric can be expressed as $\eqref{eq1}$ locally.) of class $C^\infty$ on $M$. If the integral
\begin{equation}
    \int_M K^- \mathrm{d}\sigma
\end{equation}
is finite, then $M$ is homeomorphic to the interior of a compact surface with boundary.
\end{theorem}
In order to understand the Huber's theorem, here I quote some preliminaries.


We consider an open, two-dimensional Riemannian manifold \( M \) whose metric is defined by a positive definite quadratic form
\[
ds^2 = E(\xi, \eta)d\xi^2 + 2F(\xi, \eta)d\xi d\eta + G(\xi, \eta)d\eta^2,
\]
where \( \xi \) and \( \eta \) denoting local parameters. If \( E \), \( F \) and \( G \) are sufficiently regular, then it is possible to introduce (local) \textit{isothermic parameters}, i.e., there exists a coordinate transformation \( x = x(\xi, \eta) \), \( y = y(\xi, \eta) \) such that \( E = G > 0 \), \( F = 0 \) in the \( (x, y) \)-parameter system. Then we can write
\begin{equation}\label{eq1}
    ds^2 = e^{2u(x,y)}(dx^2 + dy^2) = e^{2u} |dz|^2,
\end{equation}
putting \( z = x + iy \). Such a transformation always exists, for example, when \( E \), \( F \) and \( G \) are of class \( C^3 \), and in this case the corresponding function \( u \) is also of class \( C^3 \) (cf. A. Wintner, p. 687).


The well-known theorems of Cohn-Vossen [2] and Huber [8] assert that:
\begin{proposition}
Let \( M \) be a complete surface with the negative part of its Gaussian curvature integrable, i.e., 
\[
\int_M K_- \, dA < \infty,
\]
where
\[
K_- = 
\begin{cases} 
0 & \text{if } K > 0, \\
-K & \text{if } K \leq 0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \( M \) must be conformally equivalent to a compact Riemann surface with finitely many points deleted. Moreover
\[
\int_M K \, dA \leq 2\pi\chi(M),
\]
where \( \chi(M) \) is the Euler characteristic of \( M \). In particular, if \( \int_M |K| \, dA < \infty \), if in addition \( M \) is simply connected, then \( M \) must be conformally equivalent to the complex plane.
\end{proposition}

The following proposition was proved by Hartman in [6] for simply connected surfaces. It was later generalized by Shiohama in [15] to arbitrary complete surfaces with finite total curvature.
\begin{proposition}
Let \( M \) be a complete surface with finite total curvature. If \( K \) is the Gaussian curvature of \( M \), then we have
\[
2\pi\chi(M) - \int_M K \, dA = \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{L(r)}{r} = \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{2A(r)}{r^2}.
\]
The next result, which was proved by Hartman in [6], asserts an upper bound of the area growth of a complete surface with finite total curvature. For a higher-dimensional generalization, we would like to refer the reader to [13].
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}
Let \( M \) be a complete surface with finite total curvature. Then there exists a constant \( C_1 \), depending only on \( \int_M |K| \, dA \), such that
\[
L(\partial B_x(r)) \leq C_1 r \quad \text{and} \quad A(B_x(r)) \leq \frac{C_1}{2} r^2,
\]
for all \( x \in M \) and for all \( r > 0 \).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}
Let \( M \) be a simply connected complete noncompact surface with finite total curvature. Then there exists \( R_0 > 0 \), such that for all \( r > R_0 \), the boundary of the geodesic ball of radius \( r \) centered at \( p \) must be homeomorphic to the circle. In particular, the geodesic ball \( B_p(r) \) is homeomorphic to the disk.
\end{proposition}


\begin{theorem}[Uniformization theorem]
Suppose \( X \) is a simply connected Riemann surface. Then \( X \) can be mapped biholomorphically onto either the Riemann sphere \( \mathbb{P}^1 \), the complex plane \( \mathbb{C} \) or else the unit disk \( D \).
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
    Suppose \( X \) is a Riemann surface and \( \widetilde{X} \) is its universal covering. Since \( \widetilde{X} \) is simply connected, we may apply the Riemann Mapping Theorem to it. It is standard to call \( X \) \textbf{elliptic}, \textbf{parabolic} or \textbf{hyperbolic} depending on whether its universal covering is isomorphic to \( \mathbb{P}^1 \), \( \mathbb{C} \), or \( D \).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item The Riemann sphere \( \mathbb{P}^1 \) is elliptic.
\item The complex plane \( \mathbb{C} \), the punctured plane \( \mathbb{C}^* \) and all tori \( \mathbb{C}/\Gamma \) are parabolic.
\item Every other Riemann surface is hyperbolic.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Fischer-Colbrie-Schoen Theorem}
Peter Li's book is not clear, the following is the original paper:
\begin{theorem}[Fischer-Colbrie-Schoen]
     Let $N$ be a complete oriented 3-manifold of non-negative
scalar curvature. Let $M$ be an oriented complete stable minimal surface in $N$. 

There are two possibilities:

(i) If $M$ is compact, then $M$ is conformally equivalent to the sphere $S^2$ or $M$
is a totally geodesic flat torus $T^2$. If $S>0$ on $N$, then $M$ is conformally
equivalent to $S^2$.

(ii) If $M$ is not compact, then $M$ is conformally equivalent to the complex
plane C, or the cylinder A. If $M$ is a cylinder and the absolute total curvature
of $M$ is finite, then $M$ is flat and totally geodesic. If the scalar curnature of $N$ is everywhere positive, then $M$ cannot be a cylinder with finite total curvature.
If the Ricci curnature of $N$ is non-negative, then the assumption of finite
total curvature in (ii) can be removed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{remark}
    Note that each of the four possibilities  does occur.
\end{remark}

\section{Stokes Theorem}


Covering maps, nonorientable manifolds, singular boundary. 



Lee's deﬁnition implies that the tangent space at a boundary point is an $n$-dimensional vector space, just like the tangent spaces at interior points.
\begin{lemma}
Let $\tau \colon \mathbb{H}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ denote the inclusion map. For any $a \in \partial\mathbb{H}^n$, the differential $d \tau_a \colon T_a \mathbb{H}^n \to T_a \mathbb{R}^n$ is an isomorphism.
\end{lemma}

\section{Distance function}

\begin{theorem}
Suppose $(M,g)$ is a connected Riemannian manifold, $S \subseteq M$ is arbitrary, and $f \colon M \to [0,\infty)$ is the distance to $S$, that is, $f(x) = d_g(x, S)$ for all $x \in M$. If $f$ is continuously differentiable on some open subset $U \subseteq M \setminus S$, then $\left| \nabla f \right| = 1$ on $U$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{theorem}
Suppose $(M, g)$ is a Riemannian manifold and $f$ is a smooth local distance function on an open subset $U \subseteq M$. Then $\nabla_{\nabla f}(\nabla f) = 0$, and each integral curve of $\nabla f$ is a unit-speed geodesic.
\end{theorem}
\begin{exercise}
       Suppose $(M,g)$ is a complete, connected Riemannian manifold, $S \subseteq M$ is a closed subset, and $f \colon M \to \mathbb{R}$ is a continuous function such that $f^{-1}(0) = S$ and $f$ is smooth with unit gradient on $M \setminus S$. Prove that $f(x) = d_g(x, S)$ for all $x \in M$.
\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}
    Suppose $(M, g)$ is a Riemannian $n$-manifold, $P \subseteq M$ is a compact embedded submanifold, and $U$ is an $\epsilon$-tubular neighborhood of $P$ for some $\epsilon > 0$. For $0 < \delta < \epsilon$, define $U_{\delta}$ and $P_{\delta}$ by
\[ U_{\delta} = \{ x \in U : d_g(x, P) \leq \delta \}, \]
\[ P_{\delta} = \{ x \in U : d_g(x, P) = \delta \}. \]

(a) Prove that $U_{\delta}$ is a regular domain and $P_{\delta}$ is a compact, embedded submanifold of $M$ for each $\delta \in (0, \epsilon)$.

(b) Generalize the result of Problem 6-30 by proving that
\[ \text{Vol}(U_{\delta}) = \int_{0}^{\delta} \text{Area}(P_r) \, dr, \]
where $\text{Area}(P_r)$ denotes the $(n-1)$-dimensional volume of $P_r$ with the induced Riemannian metric.

\end{exercise}

Also in the book \textit{Riemannian Foliations} by Molino, (see proposition 3.5)

``B.Reinhart established some important properties of these foliations and, in particular, the fact that every geodesic [for a bundle-like metric] that is perpendicular at some point to a leaf remains perpendicular to all the leaves that it meets. He also showed that if the metric is complete then the leaves have the same universal covering.''



\begin{remark}
    From above, we know that it's possible to define a distance function \(r\) to a compact section of a leaf $\mathcal{F}_{p_0}$ in a Riemannian foliation $M$. Then $\nabla r$ is unit-speed geodesic and thus horizontal. 
    When $M$ has focal points wrt $\mathcal{F}_{p_0}$, the integral on the whole space will not be affected, which gives a way to derive a monotonicty formula in general Riemannian foliation setting.
\end{remark}

\begin{exercise}[Existence of a ray,from Carmo's book]
    A geodesic $\gamma: [0,\infty) \to M$ in a Riemannian manifold $M$ is called a ray starting from $\gamma(0)$ if it minimizes the distance between $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(s)$, for any $s \in (0,\infty)$. Assume that $M$ is complete, non-compact, and let $p \in M$. Show that $M$ contains a ray starting from $p$.
\end{exercise}

\begin{corollary}
     Let $E$ be an end of a complete Riemannian manifold. Suppose that for some $\nu > 1$ and $C > 0$, $E$ satisfies a Sobolev type inequality of the form
\[
\left( \int_E |u|^{2\nu} \right)^{\frac{1}{\nu}} \leq C \int_E |\nabla u|^2,
\]
for all compactly supported functions $u \in H_{c}^{1,2}(E)$ defined on $E$, then $E$ must be nonparabolic.

\end{corollary}
We know that $\mathbb{R}^2$ is parabolic, but $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\geq 3$ is nonparabolic. Compare to (note that the dimension works here)
\begin{theorem}[Gagliardo--Nirenberg--Sobolev inequality]
   Assume $1 \leq p < n$. There exists a constant $C$, depending only on $p$ and $n$, such that
\begin{equation}
\|u\|_{L^{p^*}(\mathbb{R}^n)} \leq C\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)},
\end{equation}
for all $u \in C_c^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

\end{theorem}


\begin{definition}[properly immersed submanifolds]
    An embedded submanifold with or without boundary is said to be \emph{properly embedded} if the inclusion map is proper.
\end{definition}
\begin{proposition}
If $\widetilde{M}$ is a smooth manifold with or without boundary, then an embedded submanifold $M \subseteq \widetilde{M}$ is \emph{properly embedded} if and only if it is a closed subset of $\widetilde{M}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}[cf.\href{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aim.2013.12.001}{Shun Maeta}]
    An immersed submanifold $M$ in a Riemannian manifold $N$ is said to be properly immersed if the immersion is a proper map. Here, we remark that the properness of the immersion implies the completeness of $(M,g)$.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}
    Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are topological spaces and $F: X \to Y$ is a proper map. Then $F$ takes every sequence diverging to inﬁnity in $X$ to a sequence diverging to inﬁnity in $Y$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}
    Suppose $X$ is any topological space, $Y$ is a compactly generated Hausdorff space (e.g., any subset of a manifold with or without boundary), and $F: X\to Y$ is a proper continuous map. Then $F$ is a closed map.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}
    First countable spaces and locally compact spaces are compactly generated.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}
    Suppose $F$ is a proper continuous map from a topological space to a compactly generated Hausdorff space.

(a) If $F$ is surjective, it is a quotient map.

(b) If $F$ is injective, it is a topological embedding.

(c) If $F$ is bijective, it is a homeomorphism.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}
Suppose $M$ is a smooth manifold with or without boundary, and $S \subseteq M$ is an immersed submanifold. If any of the following holds, then $S$ is embedded.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $S$ has codimension $0$ in $M$.
    \item The inclusion map $S \subseteq M$ is proper.
    \item $S$ is compact.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{lemma}[Li]
Let $M^m$ be a complete manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. Suppose $f$ is a bounded subharmonic function defined on $M$, then
\[
\lim_{\rho \to \infty} V_p^{-1}(\rho) \int_{B_p(\rho)} f(x) \, dx = \sup_M f.
\]
\end{lemma}
